question: Why don't birds get electrocuted on power lines?

claims.text: Electrical current through a body requires a difference in electrical potential across it and a conducting path.
A bird with both feet on one wire is at nearly the same electrical potential across its body, so very little current flows through it.
Touching two energized parts at different potentials, or one energized part and a grounded part, can complete a dangerous circuit through a bird.

script.short: This bird is sitting on a dangerously high-voltage wire. So why doesn't it get electrocuted? Birds are not immune to electricity. Electricity needs a route through the body, driven by a difference in electrical potential. With both feet on one wire, the bird's whole body is at almost the same potential. That leaves almost no voltage difference across it, so almost no current takes a shortcut through the bird. But touching a second wire at a different potential would bridge two electrical levels. Touching the live wire and a grounded pole creates the same danger: the body completes a path. That's the trick. One wire offers no useful route through the bird. Two connections can be deadly. Never approach or touch a power line yourself.
